q: You call setState twice in a row and expect two re-renders but only get one. Why?
options: setState is broken for multiple calls
React batches state updates in event handlers
The second call overwrites the first
You need useReducer for multiple updates
explain: React batches multiple setState calls in the same event handler into one re-render for performance.

q: Your closure inside a loop always logs the last value instead of each iteration's value. What is the fix?
options: Use var instead of let
Use let in the loop — it creates a new binding per iteration
Wrap the loop in a setTimeout
Use forEach instead of for
explain: var is function-scoped so all iterations share the same variable. let creates a new binding for each iteration so each closure captures its own value.

q: You chain .then() on a Promise but errors are silently swallowed. What are you missing?
options: A second argument to .then()
A .catch() at the end of the chain
A try/catch around the Promise
Both A and B are valid
explain: Both work. .then(onSuccess, onError) handles errors inline. .catch() at the end catches any error in the chain. Missing both means errors disappear silently.

q: You use async/await but your function still returns a Promise instead of the value. Why?
options: await is not supported in all browsers
async functions always return a Promise — await only unwraps inside the function
You need to return await instead of just return
async only works with fetch not custom Promises
explain: async functions always return a Promise. await unwraps the value inside the function but the caller still receives a Promise.

q: You use JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) to deep clone. When is this dangerous?
options: When the object has more than 10 properties
When the object contains functions, undefined, or Date objects
When the object is nested more than 3 levels deep
It is always safe
explain: JSON.stringify drops functions and undefined silently. It converts Dates to strings. Use structuredClone() for a safer native deep clone.

q: You need to run 3 API calls simultaneously and wait for all to finish. What do you use?
options: await each call one by one
Promise.race()
Promise.all()
Promise.allSettled()
explain: Promise.all() runs all promises in parallel and resolves when all succeed. It rejects immediately if any one fails.

q: Your event listener fires hundreds of times per second on scroll. The page feels slow. What is the fix?
options: Remove the event listener after first fire
Throttle or debounce the handler
Use setTimeout inside the handler
Switch from scroll to wheel event
explain: Throttle limits how often the function runs. Debounce waits until events stop before firing. Both prevent performance issues from high-frequency events.

q: You attach a click listener to 500 list items. A senior says this is a performance problem. What should you do?
options: Use querySelectorAll and loop faster
Attach one listener to the parent and use event delegation
Use addEventListener with the capture option
Batch the listeners using requestAnimationFrame
explain: Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent element. Events bubble up from children so you can handle all child clicks in one place.

q: You need to store key-value pairs where keys are objects not strings. What do you use?
options: A plain object with JSON.stringify keys
Map — it allows any type as a key
Set — it stores unique values
WeakMap — it is faster for object keys
explain: Map keys can be any type including objects and functions. Plain object keys are always coerced to strings.

q: You use setInterval to poll an API every second. The page gets slower over time. What is likely wrong?
options: setInterval is not designed for API calls
The interval is not being cleared when done
You should use setTimeout instead
The API responses are too large
explain: If the interval is never cleared it keeps running forever. Always store the interval ID and call clearInterval when done.

q: You need to find one specific item in an array. Which method is most appropriate?
options: array.filter()[0]
array.find()
array.forEach() with a break
array.includes()
explain: find() returns the first matching element and stops immediately. filter() continues through the whole array and returns all matches.

q: You want to sum all numbers in an array in one line. Which method fits best?
options: array.forEach()
array.map()
array.reduce()
array.filter()
explain: reduce() accumulates values into a single result. It's the right tool for turning an array into one value like a sum.

q: Your async function throws an error but nothing shows in the console. Why?
options: Async functions suppress all errors by default
The returned Promise was never awaited or caught
You need to use throw new Error() not throw
Errors only show if you use callbacks
explain: Unhandled Promise rejections are silent in many environments. Always await the async function or attach .catch() to handle rejections.

q: You shallow copy an object with spread and modify a nested array. The original also changes. Why?
options: Spread creates a deep copy so something else is wrong
Spread only copies top-level properties — nested objects are still referenced
Arrays cannot be spread into objects
You need to use Object.assign() instead
explain: Spread is a shallow copy. Top-level primitive values are copied but nested objects and arrays are still the same reference.

q: You use console.log inside a for loop with var and every log shows the same final value. What is the fix?
options: Use console.warn instead
Replace var with let
Wrap the loop in an async function
Use a while loop instead
explain: var is function-scoped so all iterations share one variable. By the time the logs run the loop has finished. let creates a new binding per iteration.

q: What is the difference between Promise.all() and Promise.allSettled()?
options: all() is faster, allSettled() is more accurate
all() rejects if any Promise fails, allSettled() waits for all regardless
allSettled() only works with async functions
They are identical but allSettled() has better browser support
explain: Promise.all() short-circuits on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled() always waits for every Promise and gives you each result whether fulfilled or rejected.

q: You need a function that remembers how many times it has been called. What concept makes this possible?
options: Prototypal inheritance
Closure
Hoisting
Event delegation
explain: A closure lets an inner function access variables from its outer function even after the outer function has finished. The count variable persists between calls.

q: You need to debounce a search input. What does debounce actually do?
options: Runs the function immediately then blocks for a delay
Delays execution until the user stops triggering the event
Limits how many times per second the function can run
Cancels the previous call before making a new one
explain: Debounce waits until events stop firing for a set delay before executing. Throttle limits frequency. Debounce is ideal for search inputs where you want to wait until typing pauses.

q: You call a function with call() passing a different object as this. What does this achieve?
options: It creates a copy of the function
It lets you borrow a function and run it with a different context
It permanently changes the function's this binding
It only works with class methods
explain: call() invokes a function immediately with a specified this value. bind() returns a new function with this permanently set. apply() is the same but takes arguments as an array.

q: You log Start, then setTimeout with 0ms delay, then End. What is the output order?
options: Start, Timeout, End
Timeout, Start, End
Start, End, Timeout
It depends on the browser
explain: setTimeout is asynchronous. Even with 0ms delay it goes to the callback queue. The call stack must finish executing Start and End first.

q: You need to make an object's properties unmodifiable. Which method do you use?
options: Object.lock()
Object.freeze()
Object.seal()
const obj = {}
explain: Object.freeze() prevents adding, removing, or modifying properties. Object.seal() prevents adding or removing but allows modifying existing values. const only prevents reassigning the variable.

q: Your code throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined'. What is the safest fix for deep property access?
options: Wrap every access in a try/catch
Use optional chaining: obj?.a?.b?.c
Check typeof before every access
Use Object.keys() to verify properties exist
explain: Optional chaining short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing if any part of the chain is null or undefined.

q: You want a default value when a variable is null or undefined but not when it is 0 or empty string. What operator?
options: || logical OR
?? nullish coalescing
&& logical AND
?: ternary
explain: ?? only falls back when the value is null or undefined. || falls back for any falsy value including 0 and empty string which is often not what you want.

q: You need to run cleanup code whether a function succeeds or throws. Where do you put it?
options: After the try block
In the catch block
In the finally block
In a separate function called after
explain: finally always runs regardless of whether try succeeded or catch handled an error. It's the right place for cleanup like closing connections or hiding loaders.

q: You need to check if two objects have the same properties and values. Will === work?
options: Yes === compares object contents
No === compares references not contents
Only if both objects were created the same way
Yes if you use Object.is() instead
explain: === on objects checks if they point to the same memory location not whether they have the same contents. Use JSON.stringify or a deep equality library to compare contents.
